newsitem.title: ESTONIA: YEAREND - Estonian success may lead to overheating.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Estonian success may lead to overheating.

text.p: The small Baltic state of Estonia has gained a big reputation as one of eastern Europe's most committed and successful reformers but some experts warn it may have to restrain itself in 1997 or risk an over-heating economy.
The nation of just 1.5 million people launched reforms even before quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991 and has attracted the lion's share of foreign investment in the Baltics.
But some analysts say that economic success may lead to over-heating as bank lending is growing rapidly, foreign loans are being taken and the trade deficit swells.

"The first whiff of over-heating is in the air," said Basil Zavoico, the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) resident representative in Estonia. "Prudence now will pay handsome dividends," he told Reuters.
Despite its small size, Estonia has a good reputation among international investors because of its fiscal and budgetary prudence and very open economy.

Its banking sector is one of the most advanced in eastern Europe and it has high levels of service. It had a bank crisis at the end of 1992 when the authorities took the unprecendented step of allowing banks to fold rather than bail them out.
The financial sector is increasing its sophistication and prices have risen strongly recently on the liquid stock market.
Analysts expect gross domestic product growth of three percent in 1996 and the same rate next year.
Inflation is expected to be around 15 percent and was 16.4 percent on an annual basis in November.

But economist Ardo Hansson, a future adviser to Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi and member of the central bank's board, is worried that Estonia is moving too quickly."Estonia is flying so high you cannot imagine it flying any higher," he told Reuters.
Bank lending was a key source of concern, he said. Bank lending has risen from 6.24 billion kroons at the end of October 1995 to 10.26 billion kroons at the end of October 1996.
"I wonder whether there are so many good projects (to lend to)," Hansson added.

He also noted the current account deficit was widening, fuelled by an expanding trade deficit, and that capital inflows were coming from loans by foreign banks rather than direct capital investment as before.
He said the danger of over-heating was that if the bubble burst and foreign confidence in Estonia decreased, then money could flow out just as quickly as it flowed in.
"If people start pulling their money out there would be some kind of sobering and we would have a slowdown," Hansson added. "I suspect this might happen next year," he added.
The IMF's Zavoico also said he was worried about a rising public sector deficit, boosted by local government borrowing.
He said Estonia should act early to cut spending, raise some taxes and take measures to produce a trade surplus.
He also said that land reform should be speeded up as the current state of legislation made it very hard to privatise real estate.
Hansson was optimistic for Estonia in the longer term but urged the authorities to act now to ensure smooth growth. "A soft landing is quite achievable," he said.

Leading banker Hannes Tamjaerv, chairman of the country's largest bank, Hansapank, was more optimistic. "To my mind there is a theoretical danger of over-heating but recognising the danger is already half the solution," Tamjaerv told Reuters.
